transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Please tell me what brings you in today — is there something specific that’s been troubling you or that you’d like to talk about?

Well, I suppose I'm here because... well, my family pushed me to come. They think I’m overworking myself or getting too stressed out, but they just aren't looking at the facts. I’m a computer systems analyst, so my entire day is spent looking at data, finding anomalies, tracking down where things break in a system. That’s how my brain works, it's what I'm trained to do. So when my father passed away, naturally, I wanted to organize everything, get the estate in order, all of that. But the more I looked into the documentation, the more things just didn't add up. 

I know everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and those donation emails all line up perfectly. My sister, my mom, they all tell me to just accept it and move on, that it's just standard paperwork. But... but when I actually sit down and compare the timestamps—and I mean really look at them, tracking the routing data down to the minute—they don't match the official timeline. And there are missing attachments, too. I've found several emails that clearly say 'see attached file' or reference a document, but there's absolutely nothing attached in the archives. I've mapped it all out. 

And it's not just the digital trail. When I try to ask about these discrepancies, the way certain community members just completely avoid my questions... they look away, they get defensive, or they suddenly make excuses to leave the room. It’s... well, it’s obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death. I just can't understand why everyone else is ignoring the evidence right in front of them when the data clearly shows something was altered. I actually have the spreadsheets right here on my phone if you want to see the gaps I'm talking about...
Do you believe that certain people or organizations are intentionally hiding information from you or working together to cover up what really happened surrounding your father's death?

Yes! Yes, exactly. I mean, it's not even a matter of belief at this point, it's just looking at the raw data. Like I was saying, I know everyone—my mom, my sister, even my uncle who usually has a really good head on his shoulders—they all keep telling me that the hospital records and those donation emails all line up perfectly. They just want to trust the system, you know? It's easier for them to grieve if they just believe the neat little bow that was tied around his passing. 

But when I actually sit down and cross-reference the server timestamps... and I'm talking about the metadata, the routing paths that most people don't even know how to look for... and then I combine that with those missing attachments I mentioned, it’s just undeniable. 

And it's not just the digital side, which is what really gets to me. It’s the human element. Like, just last week, I ran into Mr. Henderson from the local community board—he knew my dad for twenty years, they volunteered together—and when I brought up the specific discrepancies I found in the Tuesday timeline, he literally couldn't look me in the eye. He just mumbled something about being late for a committee meeting and practically sprinted to his car. It’s the way certain community members just completely avoid my questions like that. They get this panicked, guarded look the second I bring up the paperwork. 

So, yes, when you put all that together—the fact that I can prove the timestamps were altered, the missing files, the way people are physically acting around me—it’s completely obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death. I mean, why else would they scrub the email attachments? Why else would people run away from a simple, logical question? It’s a coordinated effort, plain and simple, and I feel like I'm the only one willing to do the actual work to expose it. If you just let me pull up row 47 on my spreadsheet here, I can show you exactly where the server handoff was intercepted...
Outside of the issues you've described around your father's death, do you ever find yourself noticing other patterns or hidden meanings in everyday events that other people don't seem to pick up on?

No, no, not at all. I mean, I think you might be misunderstanding where I'm coming from with all this. I'm not sitting around looking for, you know, secret codes in my cereal box or thinking the government is tracking my commute to work or something. That’s just not who I am. I’m a very logical person. Like I said, I’m a systems analyst, I have a bachelor's degree in computer science, so my whole life is built on structured, predictable logic. 

If I go to the grocery store, it's just a grocery store. If I get an email from my boss, it's just a normal email about our server migrations. I don't read into things that aren't there, and I don't look for hidden meanings in everyday life because, frankly, everyday life is pretty mundane. Most people just go about their business. My friends would tell you I'm probably the most pragmatic, straightforward guy they know. 

So, no, I don't see patterns in random, everyday events. But... but see, that's exactly why this situation with my father's estate is so glaring to me! It stands out specifically *because* I don't just invent patterns out of thin air. I only see what the raw data shows me. And the data here... I mean, it's not a "hidden meaning" if it's a measurable, verifiable fact. If you just look at the packet routing logs I managed to pull, you'd see it's a literal, physical gap in the digital record. It’s right there in black and white. I'm not making leaps of logic, I'm just following the breadcrumbs someone carelessly left behind. If you just give me a second to unlock my screen, I can show you the exact directory where the files were purged...

Have there ever been times when you experienced things like hearing voices that others don’t hear, believing things that others find strange or untrue, or speaking in a way that others had difficulty understanding?

No, definitely not. I mean, hearing voices? That sounds like something from a movie, or... or someone who really needs serious psychiatric help, you know? Like someone who has completely lost touch with reality. That is absolutely not me. I've never heard voices, I've never seen things that aren't there, none of that. My hearing and vision are perfectly fine. I get my eyes checked every year because I stare at screens for ten hours a day, and my prescription hasn't changed in three years. 

And as for speaking in a way people don't understand... well, sometimes I might use technical jargon when I'm explaining a complex system architecture to a client who isn't super tech-savvy, and they might look at me a little blankly until I break it down into layman's terms. Like if I start talking about latency issues in a cloud-based SQL database, a project manager might glaze over. But that's just professional communication gaps, not... not whatever you're implying. I speak very clearly, very logically. I'm always very precise with my words. 

And believing things others find strange... well, we've already covered that. My family thinks my findings about my dad's estate are "strange" or "untrue," but as I've been trying to explain, they aren't beliefs. They are facts. They are data points. Just because they don't want to look at the spreadsheet doesn't mean the spreadsheet isn't real. It just means they are choosing to ignore reality, whereas I am the only one actually looking at it. But no, I don't have any bizarre beliefs about aliens or mind control or whatever else you might be checking off on your clipboard right now. I just want people to look at the actual, physical evidence I've collected. Speaking of which, if you look at this email header here... wait, let me just scroll down... see this IP address? It routes through a completely different server than the hospital's main exchange...

Have there been times when you felt your mood was significantly different from usual—like unusually down, hopeless, or even unusually energetic or irritable—alongside these concerns about the events around your father's death?

No, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, look, am I frustrated? Yes, absolutely. But calling it 'unusually irritable' makes it sound like I'm just flying off the handle for no reason, like some kind of irrational mood swing. If I get annoyed, it's a completely proportional, logical response to the fact that I am presenting people with literal, verifiable metadata and they are treating me like I'm speaking a foreign language. Anyone would be irritated if they were holding the absolute proof of a cover-up and everyone just kept looking the other way. 

And as for being down or hopeless... no. I mean, obviously, I was sad when my dad passed. That's just normal human grief. Anyone would be sad about losing their father, especially given how close we were and how sudden the whole thing was. But I'm not sitting around crying all day or unable to get out of bed, if that's what you mean. Actually, I feel highly motivated right now. I'm incredibly focused. I get up at 6:00 AM every single day, I make my coffee, I log into my work VPN, I handle my server tickets and team meetings, and then in the evenings, I dedicate my time to parsing these logs. I'm functioning perfectly. 

I'm not 'unusually energetic' either, like I don't have some kind of boundless, crazy energy. I get tired just like anyone else. I just drink a little extra espresso when I'm compiling the data because the hospital's portal limits how many queries I can run per hour, so I have to time my scripts perfectly to bypass the throttle, which means staying up a bit late sometimes to monitor the downloads. But my baseline mood? It's completely stable. It's flat. I'm an analyst, doctor. I kind of have to be even-keeled to do my job. You can't write clean code or design a stable system architecture if you're an emotional wreck. 

So, no, there are no mood swings here. No depression, no mania, whatever you want to call it. Just a very rational, steady determination to get to the bottom of this. Which, again, I could easily demonstrate if we just look at the discrepancies in the Tuesday timeline... I actually have a pivot table right here that charts out the exact minute the file sizes changed...

Have there ever been times in your life, other than around your father's death, when you strongly believed something was true based on patterns or data you saw, even though others could not see those patterns or agreed that the data didn't support your belief?

No, never. I mean, absolutely not. If you look at my track record, both professionally and personally, there is zero history of me, you know, going off the reservation or chasing ghosts. Like I said, I'm an analyst. My entire job, literally what I get paid to do every single day, is to look at data and find the actual, verifiable root cause of a system error. And when I find it, I document it, I present it to the QA team, and they verify it. It's a consensus based on facts. 

Like, just last year, we had this massive memory leak in one of our legacy applications at work. The client was losing their mind, the project managers were convinced it was a hardware failure on the server rack, and nobody could figure it out. I spent three days digging through the stack traces. Three days of just raw, unfiltered error logs. And I found the pattern—a recursive loop in the code that was only triggering under very specific user-load conditions. Now, initially, the senior developers didn't see it. They thought I was looking in the completely wrong directory. But I didn't just 'strongly believe' it based on some gut feeling or invisible pattern. I ran the simulation, I generated the crash report, and I showed them exactly where the memory was spiking. And you know what happened? They looked at the data, they saw the math, they realized I was right, and we patched it. 

So, no, I don't have a history of seeing things that aren't there or clinging to beliefs that the data doesn't support. If the data doesn't support it, I drop it. That's the scientific method. That's basic logic. I've never been the guy who cries wolf or spins wild theories. I've always been the guy who brings the receipts. 

Which, again, is why it is so incredibly frustrating to me that my family is treating me like I've suddenly lost my mind over my dad's estate. This isn't a pattern of behavior for me. I've never done anything like this before because I've never *encountered* a situation like this before! If I had found a discrepancy in my taxes five years ago, I would have called the IRS, showed them the math, and fixed it. This is no different, except the stakes are my father's legacy and the hospital's blatant tampering with the records. If you just look at my work history, you'd see I am incredibly reliable. I don't make mistakes with data. And I'm definitely not making a mistake now. I mean, if you just let me pull up the secondary drive I brought with me... I actually have a whole folder of my past performance reviews and project post-mortems if you really need to establish a baseline of my credibility before we look at the hospital logs...

And when I find it, I document it, I present it to the QA team, and they verify it. It's a consensus based on facts. 

Like, just last year, we had this massive memory leak in one of our legacy applications at work. The client was losing their mind, the project managers were convinced it was a hardware failure on the server rack, and nobody could figure it out. I spent three days digging through the stack traces. Three days of just raw, unfiltered error logs. And I found the pattern—a recursive loop in the code that was only triggering under very specific user-load conditions. Now, initially, the senior developers didn't see it. They thought I was looking in the completely wrong directory. But I didn't just 'strongly believe' it based on some gut feeling or invisible pattern. I ran the simulation, I generated the crash report, and I showed them exactly where the memory was spiking. And you know what happened? They looked at the data, they saw the math, they realized I was right, and we patched it. 

So, no, I don't have a history of seeing things that aren't there or clinging to beliefs that the data doesn't support. If the data doesn't support it, I drop it. That's the scientific method. That's basic logic. I've never been the guy who cries wolf or spins wild theories. I've always been the guy who brings the receipts. 

Which, again, is why it is so incredibly frustrating to me that my family is treating me like I've suddenly lost my mind over my dad's estate. This isn't a pattern of behavior for me. I've never done anything like this before because I've never *encountered* a situation like this before! If I had found a discrepancy in my taxes five years ago, I would have called the IRS, showed them the math, and fixed it. This is no different, except the stakes are my father's legacy and the hospital's blatant tampering with the records. If you just look at my work history, you'd see I am incredibly reliable. I don't make mistakes with data. And I'm definitely not making a mistake now. I mean, if you just let me pull up the secondary drive I brought with me... I actually have a whole folder of my past performance reviews and project post-mortems if you really need to establish a baseline of my credibility before we look at the hospital logs...
